tagline.text: An 1893 US Navy armored cruiser wreck resting on the floor of Subic Bay

location.label: Location
location.text: Waters off Olongapo port, Subic Bay (near the Kalaklan River mouth)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱3,900–6,000 (for two boat dives; varies by operator)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Clark International Airport (CRK) or Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL)

children.text: The wreck of the US Navy armored cruiser USS New York, scuttled by the Navy off Olongapo port in Subic Bay in 1941. Her roughly 110 m hull lies on its port side, with 8-inch guns and a huge propeller, making this an advanced-level wreck dive.

USS New York (ACR-2) was a US Navy armored cruiser commissioned in Philadelphia in August 1893. She was about 117 m long and served as flagship of Admiral Sampson's squadron during the Spanish–American War. She was later renamed Saratoga in 1911 and Rochester in 1917, was decommissioned at Cavite in 1933, and then served as a workshop and supply ship in Subic Bay. On December 24, 1941, the US Navy scuttled her to keep her from falling into Japanese hands, and today she is one of Subic Bay's best-known wreck dive sites. The ship lies on her port (left) side, and about 110 m of the hull is said to remain relatively intact. The turreted deck guns and the large propeller at the stern are the main attractions. In 1967 the US Navy used demolition charges to lower the wreck, and the blast damage is still visible in the midsection. Over time, corals and marine life have settled on the structure, and it now also works as an artificial reef.
Depth figures differ by source. The top of the hull is at about

and the seabed is at about 30 m, while many dive shops quote 17–27 m. The wreck lies close to the mouth of the Kalaklan River, so currents are often strong and visibility is often poor, which makes it suitable for experienced divers with Advanced Open Water certification or higher. Entering the hull requires technical or wreck-specialty training. Compared with the El Capitan wreck, another Subic Bay wreck, USS New York is larger, deeper and heavier with history. But with its demanding visibility and currents, it is less a wreck for everyone and more one for experienced divers to take on. For an overview of diving in Subic Bay, see also
Subic Bay

Knowing the ship's history makes the dive more interesting. Launched in 1891, USS New York was flagship of the North Atlantic Squadron and the centerpiece of the fleet Admiral Sampson led in the Spanish–American War. To free her name for newer battleships she was called Saratoga in 1911 and Rochester in 1917, and she escorted convoys during World War I. In 1920 she was redesignated CA-2, and in 1933 she was decommissioned at Cavite. The old warship, once used in Subic Bay as a workshop and storage ship, sank for the last time at today's dive site. The wreck is said to lie in the Olongapo port area, between Alava Pier and the end of the former Subic airport runway. Because it is close to commercial shipping lanes, diving is allowed only with permission from the port authority and through approved boats and divemasters. This is the biggest difference from other Subic Bay wrecks, so independent travelers should always arrange the dive through a local dive shop.

Subic Bay also has many other wrecks at recreational depths, such as El Capitan (USS Majaba), San Quentin, Oryoku Maru, Seian Maru, a landing ship (LST) and USS Lanikai, as well as technical-depth Japanese wrecks such as Kyo Maru and Banshu Maru, and aircraft wrecks. We recommend staying a few days and getting a feel for shallower wrecks with steadier visibility before taking on USS New York.

Turreted guns remain on the deck and make for the signature scene of the dive. It is said the ship was sunk to keep these guns out of Japanese hands. The area around the guns is deep and visibility can drop quickly, so a flashlight helps. Because the hull lies on its left side, the deck appears tilted, so follow your guide to avoid losing your sense of direction.

A large propeller, taller than a person, remains near the stern. It gives the best sense of the ship's size and is a popular spot for photos and video. It is close to the seabed, so silt is easily stirred up and you need to pay attention to buoyancy control. It is on the deeper side and your no-decompression time runs down quickly, so check your dive computer often.

blocks.title: A huge hull about 110 m long

children.text: The wreck is so large that it is hard to see all of it in a single dive. It is among the larger wrecks in Subic Bay. The usual approach is to move along one side with a guide and visit the main points.
Marks of the 1967 work in which the US Navy used demolition charges to lower the hull remain in the midsection. Torn plates and collapsed structure show the passage of time on the wreck.
Corals and marine life live on the plating and structures, and the hull works as a reef. On days with good visibility you can see fish around the hull.

Said to have been a warship that served as flagship in the Spanish–American War, the wreck is very popular with divers interested in history. Learning the ship's story before the dive makes it far more interesting.

blocks.title: A benchmark of Subic Bay wreck diving

children.text: Subic Bay is packed with wrecks and is considered one of the centers of wreck diving in the Philippines. USS New York is a symbol in both size and history, so some wreck fans visit Subic for this one site. However, on days with poor visibility there may be less to see than you hoped, so allow a day or two of slack in your schedule.

items.title: Half-day wreck dive
items.subtitle: From meeting at the port to the boat dive

children.text: Meet at a dive shop in Subic or Olongapo, check your equipment and attend the briefing. Entry time is adjusted to field conditions because of currents and ship traffic.
Travel by boat to the wreck site. As a rule, you go with an operator and divemaster approved by the port authority.
Start by seeing the guns and deck from the upper part of the hull, then, if you feel good, move toward the stern propeller.
Finish your safety stop, surface and take a surface interval. The second dive is sometimes at the same site or at another wreck.
Entry times can vary greatly with the operator and sea conditions that day, so treat the times above as an example only.

items.title: Two-day, one-night wreck itinerary
items.subtitle: Seeing two wrecks in a row in Subic

children.text: Arrive in Subic Freeport or Olongapo, drop your bags at your hotel and have the dive shop check your certification card and logbook. Rest while looking around inside Subic Bay.
Reconfirm the next day's entry time and boat departure time with the operator and turn in early.
Warm up with a first dive on a relatively shallow wreck, then decide on the USS New York dive after checking your condition and the visibility.
Because of ship traffic, the allowed entry window is sometimes set around midday. In one case it was between 11:00 AM and 12:30 PM.
In one case a single dive around the hull lasted about 40 minutes. Because of the depth, your time runs down quickly.
A long-distance bus from Manila to Olongapo or Subic often takes roughly 3 hours. It varies greatly with traffic, so check locally.
Some dive shops offer pickup from Manila, so ask when you book.
Clark International Airport (CRK) is relatively close to Subic. You can also travel by car from Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL).
From the airport to Subic can take more than 1 hour by car.
The wreck is in the waters near Olongapo port, so you go by boat. It is hard for individuals to find a boat, so going through a dive shop is the norm.
Permission from the port authority and an approved boat and divemaster are required, so always go through a local operator.
The Subic Bay wrecks are comfortable to dive in the dry season, November–May. However, because the wreck is near the mouth of the Kalaklan River, visibility can get even worse after the river swells.
In the rainy season, rain and wind can limit boat operations, so check with your operator before departure.

Even in the dry season, visibility varies greatly from day to day. Descriptions of 5–15 m are common, but there is a record of under 1 m in January 2026, so lower your expectations for visibility. It is best to avoid the day after rain.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: The most comfortable time for diving. Mornings and evenings can be chilly.
The sea is generally calm. The midday sun is strong, so prepare shade on the boat.
Visibility worsens after rain and boats can be canceled.

Staying in Subic Freeport or downtown Olongapo keeps you close to the dive shops. Dive schedules often start early in the morning, so it is better to stay nearby the night before. A day trip from Manila is tight on travel and entry time. One account says leaving Manila before dawn and arriving after about 4 hours, so we recommend one night.
You can get meals in Subic Freeport and Olongapo. A light meal after diving is recommended.
Take on this wreck only with Advanced Open Water certification or higher and recent diving experience.
Bring a flashlight. The depths and the shadow of the hull are dark, and visibility is often poor.
Take care with your fin kicks and buoyancy control so you do not stir up silt.
Do not enter the hull without specialty training.
Many descriptions say visibility is about 5–15 m, but on some days it is under 1 m depending on weather and river water.
This is an area with heavy ship traffic, so entry times can change. Leave some slack in your schedule.
Carry a dive computer and keep to your safety stop.
When booking a dive shop, ask about certification level, number of recent dives, equipment rental and whether they arrange the port permit.
On days with poor visibility, do not push to go deeper and follow your guide's judgment.
Subic has many other wrecks, so do not build your schedule around USS New York alone, and talk with your operator in advance about switching sites according to weather and visibility.
This is an advanced-level wreck with strong currents and possibly poor visibility. Do not penetrate the hull without specialty training.
Near the river mouth, currents can run strong.
Inside the hull it is tight, dark and silty, and visibility can drop to zero in an instant.
Permission from the port authority and an approved boat and divemaster are required. Check the latest notices on the rules.
The hull plating is sharp and old, so do not touch it.
A diver death on this wreck in 2001 was reported. Do not push your limits.
Dive insurance (such as DAN) is helpful in an accident. Ask the operator where the nearest decompression chamber is.
Another wreck dive site in Subic Bay, reached by boat. It is often combined in the same day's schedule, so ask the operator.
An area packed with a variety of things to do at the Freeport, not just wreck diving.
An island at the mouth of Subic Bay where you can enjoy a beach and relaxation. Check travel times by car and boat locally.
